Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Bernie wrote:
>>I'm wondering if Succubus Club may be banned after the Nationals,
considering the new interest in deal making with SC often borders
on collusion.>>

Right. Collusion. Could someone please accurately define "collusion", and what
it means in relation to VTES?

For years, people have throwm around the word "collusion", and I have always
taken it to mean, effectively, two or more people organizing before a
tournament to make one of them win by working together, regardless of the table
dynamic. Thus, if I go to a tournament with Jason and Eric, and before hand we
all agree that I will get into the finals, and the other two will give up their
own games to make me win, and during the tournament, the other two do things
that are specifically bad for them just to help me (like, say, when Jason is my
prey, he ousts himself quickly, never blocks me, and in no way tries to defend
himself, just so I get the 6 pool and VP for ousting him), that is collusion.

On the other hand, making deals in the middle of a tournament with people you
have had no discussion with before hand, regardless of the deal, cannot be
collusion, by defenition. If you don't discuss the collusion before the game,
and you don't plan from the outset to throw your game to make someone else win,
that isn't collusion.

Collusion, as I understand it, specifically deals with out of game discussion
and pre-meditated game throwing. People from the same playgroup driving to a
convention, all of whom agree to do everything they can to get player X into
the finals, and then all doing stupid things in a game to help player X, even
if player X is their predator or prey. That is collusion. Making a deal with
some guy across the table you just met to split the table 2/3, even if it is
not such a good deal for you, cannot be considered collusion, as there was no
pre-meditation on the subject.

Am I off base here?

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Matt wrote:
>>Ok.. hows this for an example. I build my deck around the following premise:
I get
out a succubus club turn 1, and tell my prey that I'll help him get 3 vp if he
gives me 2. So, on turn one, before anyone has done anything, I make this
deal.>>

Sounds good to me--you have a deck that is designed to get 2VPs. Just like most
intercept decks.

>>Is this illegal? By Peter's definiton, how could it be?>>

I don't think that it is.

>>There's no collusion going on. By the VEKN Tourney rules yes it is.>>

How so? You are maximizing your VPs. If you can't reasonably get more than 2VPs
in any case with the deck in question, then the 3/2 table split deal you make
is an attempt to maximize your VPs, and has no "outside of game considerations"
aspect at all. You would make this 3/2 table split with anyone, regardless of
who they were, as that is what your deck does.

Don't get me wrong here--I think that the Succubus Club *should* be banned from
tournament play, but it isn't yet, and that isn't the issue here.

>>So having the Chairman of VEKN subscribing to Peter's definition of
Collusion, does that not require a change in the VEKN tourney rules?>>

I don't see that Goudie's agreement with me is in any way contrary to the VEKN
tournament rules.

>>Where does this fall in the whole collusion argument. The situations
described by
Peter are clearly illegal. So is mine, but for different reasons I think.>>

But I don't think that the situation you present is illegal. I make 3/2 table
split deals all the time. I don't do it because I happen to like the guy I'm
sitting next to, or 'cause he is from my play group, I do so because, at the
time I make the deal, it seems like the best way to maximize my VPs. Does this
occasionally piss someone off who gets screwed by the deal I make? Sure. All
the time, actually, but I'm not making the deal due to out of game
considerations--I am making the deal to maximize my victory points. The
situation you present above (with the SC deck) seems perfectly legal--you are
attempting to maximize your VPs, and doing so without pre-game discussion, and
without throwing your game position to arbitrarily make someone else win the
game with no concern for your own game.

>>If you are arguing against the use of the word "collusion" Peter then ok, I
understand.>>

No, I'm not arguing against it--I'm hoping to get a standard defenition for the
term, so that everyone will be talking about the same thing in these
conversations. I think that specifically the term "collusion" refers to the
situation I presented at the start of this thread. It is being used, however,
as a blanket term to indite any sort of play that invloves more than one player
and seems in some way questionable, which I don't think it actually should be
used for. As the VEKN rules specifically disallow "collusion", we should all
know what "collusion" is before we start accusing folks of it, and I don't
think that there is currently a consensus as to what the term means yet.

>>But how do you tell when a deal is pre-meditated and when it is not?>>

You can't. That is why I think the whole concept of legislated "anti-collusion"
rules is a questionable concept, at best. However, if it does exist, and actual
collusion is actually ocurring, you can usually figure it out (dumb,
inappropriate game play among folks from the same play group, for instance).
Sure, a couple of total strangers can get together to pull off an elaborate
collusion sting operation that can't be traced, but A) that seems highly
unlikely and B) this is a goofy card game about pretend vampires, not Vegas.

>>In the situation I describe, really, how DO you tell?>>

Assuming that game play and the deal in question seems reasonably sound (i.e. I
can see the logic in it), I'll assume that the folks I am playing with are on
the up and up.

It seems *possible* that at some point I could be taken by an elaborate
collusion scheeme, but it also seems so unlikely that I'm not going to worry
about it. Obvious collusion is obvious. Inobvious collusion is impossible to
detect.



I think you're accurately pointing out some potential semantic confusion between
two separate issues. But I'd like to point out that this doesn't mean what Bernie
was talking about isn't a problem.

Never mind the preagreed-apon out-of-tournament deal intended to throw victory
points to a single player or even to split tables by working together right from
the start, in the absence of any consideration of the existing table dynamics. That
*is* illegal, if I understand the rules correctly. So Bernie could not be referring
to that kind of behavior.

What Bernie is talking about, though not currently illegal (as long as players can
credibly make the argument that they have gotten the most out of their position by
dealing), is still highly irritating and IMO (and probably in the opinion of a lot
of players) wouldn't be missed in the slightest. I think the problem is that, like an
overpowered card, if you can make such a deal, there's no incentive not to. Frequently,
two players correctly positioned and/or using complimentary decks, can make a deal so
powerful as to become unstoppable. I've yet to hear about the guy who said, "Whoops,
that was a dumb deal for me to make in retrospect!" about a victory point split like
that. (Except perhaps for the LA Qualifier finals, where it wasn't the deal that
failed, it was just the players who lost entirely by brain fart.) It's not like
someone's ever likely to pull a card out of their ass that punishes the pair for
dealing with each other.

The problem is is that much though we'd like people to play entirely in their own
direct interests at all time, it's just impossible to draw some kind of line that makes
this sort of VP splitting illegal. You can suspect it but you can never prove it.
Two things I'd like done, though:

1) Adopt the games-won score as the primary method of determine tournament finalist
as being currently tested by Robert Goudie. I'd love to see it tweaked, though, so that
players splitting a 2-2 score get less than one-half of a game won each. Any tie for
victory points fewer than 2 should not grant any games won to any of the players.

and

2) Ban Succubus Club. Though there are legitimate uses for this card, it's most
noticeable effect on the tournament game is to facilitate this kind of stuff. Highly
competitive tournaments will be a lot better off without this card.

Take this two steps and I'll bet we hear a lot less about this situation in the future.

Fred

Messages.Author: Ian Lee
Messages.Body:


I believe that collusion is broader than what you described. In addition,
there is a way of playing that probably doesn't fit under a technical
definition but amounts to the same.

It is not necessary to form an agreement before a tournament. It is sufficient
to enter into a secret, out of game agreement at some point during the
tournament which gives you and another player an advantage. Secret being key
to the dictionary definition, but I'd also include open agreements if they have
a basis in out of game considerations (which, if done correctly, are impossible
to prove).

Nor is it necessary for there to be an agreement to throw games or to sacrifice
one's own position wholely for another player. It is sufficient to advantage
your partner in even minor ways (less blatant aid should also make collusion
impossible to prove).

Now, a very similar tactic to true collusion is to advantage another player
using out of game considerations, regardless as to whether that player realizes
it, though with no agreement, it probably doesn't qualify as true collusion.

One of the reasons I gave up on B5 majors was that I found myself using the
last tactic naturally. All I had to do was keep in mind how my actions would
affect the scores of my friends and my other opponents (and mine too, of
course). Now, B5 has always been far better suited to collusion, but I've read
Magic reports with blatant references to helping friends at the expense of
others (with it being considered a normal tournament practice), so it isn't
even limited to multiplayer CCGs.

It seems to me then that if 2 players at a 5 player table that are striking a
deal to split Victory Points 2:3, that one player will obviously not be
fullfilling their ability to gain the most VP's (as one player will be
agreeing to take only 2 of the 3 VP's).

While I would agree that deal making & table talk are a stategic piece
of V:TES, haggling and cutting deals over VP's strikes me as
unsportsmanlike conduct.
That being a personal opinion.

If you have two "name" players at a table with 3 newbies, it's rather
insulting (and arrogant) when the 2 aforementioned players cut a deal
splitting a table yet to be won. And odds are that the "name" players
will be familiar enough with each others skills/decks to make such
a deal pan-out (no disrespect to the newbies).

So as far as I'm concerned,
Collusion = Cutting deals with other players to net "x" VP's.
Not Collusion = Cutting deals to create player advantage

What's the difference you ask? Here's an example:

1. Player A to Player C "If I switch places with Player B, it will be
in your best interest"

2. Player A to Player C "If you support my switching with Player B,
I can take her out and will then roll over to give you my victory point"

Please understand that my verbage in the examples are probably
not the best, I was simply trying to capture the difference in
spirit between two such conversations.

At any non-VEKN sponsored tourney I run in the future, I may
impliment a house rule that no deals regarding Victory Points
may be discussed during a game. If players are trying to cut
deals outside of game, why should I care as most seating
is randomized so such deals are probably never going to
achieve fruition.

or break a deal so that they get the most, theoretically possible VPs -
because of the inevitable loops this creates.

Messages.Body:
Aaron wrote:
>>Your table split deals made me highly unhappy. I though I was a good sport

I do too--I enjoyed playing with you, in both games. I was just pointing out

>>But then I would say that if you had been playing a deck with forward power
you wouldn't have had to make those kind of deals?>>

I have a deck with forward power, but sometimes I have to make deals to get
anywhere. In that first game (vs the guy with the Lasombra bruise/bleed deck
when you were my predator), I had every reason to believe that my prey had
enough combat to make it not so worth my while to mindlessly attack him (his
first 2 or 3 discards were Bum's Rush, Torn Signpost, and some other Pot card).
Thus, rather than attacking someone whocould fight back, get myself killed, and
then get ousted by you, I made a 3/2 split deal (which worked out as a 2/2
split deal, which was even better). In retrospect, I probably could have killed
him (he had less combat than I thought--thos first few discards were either
*incredibly* shrewed or a total fluke), but at the time I made the deal, I was
convinced it was the best option, and once I made the deal, I wasn't going to
break it. In that second game, I didn't make any deals at all for the first
half of the game--I was plowing full hog into my prey. Granted, I tried to
convince him to oust the Viscisitude deck before I killed him, but he was
unwilling to play. But then you switched our seats and stole all my hard work
and VP. After that, my job was to kill you (what is the point of making threats
that are idle when you can live up to them?), as I assured you would happen
before you took my seat. Heck, I even gave you the option of not switching
seats with me, just so I wouldn't have to kill you. After that, I made a deal
with Robin so that we both ended up with VPs, which worked out to both our
benefits.

>>It seems like most of the decks that are most offensive tend to *require*
some kind of deal to function at all.>>

Sure. My Rush deck doesn't require deal making. Sometimes I make them 'cause it
benefits me. Most of the time, however, I just kill stuff and get VPs. Just
when my prey is some sort of deck that can fight with me (like another Rush
deck), there is no percentage at all in fighting--we both lose. Thus, we make a
deal, and both benefit.

>>That deck does what it's supposed to, but not what the game intends to.>>

Perhaps, perhaps not. I agree, however, that the Succubus Club should not be
allowed in Tournament play for many reasons, but that is not the issue here.

>>You would have thought you could have swept the table, if you were playing a
table sweeping deck.(sorry, on the general rush combat is not a table
sweeper just yet)>>

You are incorrect. I regularly get 4VPs with that deck. It all depends on what
decks I sit down with. John Bell got into the finals of the Qualifier on 8VPs.
Rush decks are perfectly capable of sweeping (at least 4 VPs) a table.

>>Playing decks that cannot win a lot of VP makes it easy
to need deals. Playing decks designed to win means, to me, that if no one
else wants to work with you then you are just playing the game the regular
way.>>

I play Rush decks because A) not enough other folks do, and I got something to
prove and B) 'cause I can get away with making deals (I have the Smack Talk
discipline at superior). Sometimes I have to make deals to get VPs. Sometimes
not.

>>Basically I feel cheated, because I wanted to play a game where the idea is
a balance of everyone attack left while being attacked right.>>

But not all decks work that way. Sure, some do. Some very effective ones do.
But other decks don't. Intercept decks, for instance, are often completely
ineffective at hurting their prey. Rush decks work however they want, and the
good ones still win.

>>Because someone makes a deal to ignore the most basic principle of the game
they are devaluing the experience. If you don't want to attack left, why not
play
something where you don't have to?>>

I'm a big fan of attacking left, but if attacking left is just going to get me
killed, why not try another alternative? Say you are playing a Malk S+B deck.
Your deck can't do anything but bleed big at stealth. Your prey happens to be a
deck, just by sheer luck, with 23 Deflections and 15 Wakes in it. Are you going
to mindlessly attempt to bleed them, so you can sweep the table for them?
Attack left is how the game works and a good idea, but not if it is going to
get you killed.

>>Maybe I just have problems because when I create decks I expect someone's
predator(the person who should be trying to kill them) to, you guessed it,
try to kill them!>>

I build decks to kill my prey. Most of the time, I kill my prey. You played
with me in two games. In one, I made a table split deal, 'cause if I didn't, I
thought I was just going to lose. In the other, I did my very darndest to kill
my prey, until you switched seats with me and stole my VP, at which point, the
whole game just flew out the window (as I warned you before hand it would) for
everyone involved. Do you not see the logic behind what happened in both of
these games?

>>I could be wrong...and the number of victory points in a tournament, overall,
is probably far more important then the basic principle of the game.>>

Deal making is a basic principle of the game--it is designed to be multi
player, and all interactive multiplayer games are, by defenition, political.

>>(venting not against Peter, but against the idea that pacifying your
predator with 2 VP so you can have 3 would ever be a good idea, and for the
people who's game is ruined by someone essentially without a predator)>>

People sit down all the time effectively without a predator. If your predator
is a run of the mill intercept deck, what pressure is being put on you if you
are playing a full forward deck? If your predator is a horse abuse bloat deck,
what kind of pressure are they going to put on you?

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <20010801161636...@ng-ba1.aol.com>, BernieTime
<berni...@aol.com> writes

>If I was unclear, would it not be collusion

Since this occurs in-game, with in-game considerations, it is *not*
collusion.

Collusion involves out of game deal making and considerations.

Please do not confuse collusion with non-winning deals. The two are
*very* different.

> if a player at start
>of game accepts a deal with another player with an
>intended split which would only result in that player
>only gaining 2 Vp's?

If the judge is of the opinion that this is a winning deal, it would not
have to be ruled out under the "winning deal" rules. At the start of a
game, it might be difficult to establish that the two players were in a
position to know this.

Messages.Author: Johan Lundstrom
Messages.Body:
Frederick Scott <fre...@netcom.com> wrote:

>Two things I'd like done, though:

>1) Adopt the games-won score as the primary method of determine tournament finalist
>as being currently tested by Robert Goudie. I'd love to see it tweaked, though, so that
>players splitting a 2-2 score get less than one-half of a game won each. Any tie for
>victory points fewer than 2 should not grant any games won to any of the players.

>and

>2) Ban Succubus Club. Though there are legitimate uses for this card, it's most
>noticeable effect on the tournament game is to facilitate this kind of stuff. Highly
>competitive tournaments will be a lot better off without this card.

>Take this two steps and I'll bet we hear a lot less about this situation in the future.

I totally agree. The current tournament rules encourages people to
play for the VPs, while the rules *say* they should play for the wins.
Having conflicting goals on what the player is supposed to play like
and what is actually in his best interest to do is a breeding ground
for dishonesty. If players are supposed to play for wins, then the
tournament rules should value wins, not VPs.

Doing things like your Case 1 would eliminate the 3-2 table split. I
agree that a two draws should be valued at less than one win, or there
will be an incentive for even table splits. It would also lessen the
need for table-sweepers, which is a good thing, IMO.

And the Succubus Club has no business in a tournament. It just screams
out "Abuse me!" Collusion is easy enough as it is - there's no need to
help it along.
